Shell theorem of Newtonian gravitation states:

* A spherical shell pulls an outside point as if all its mass were at the center.
* any inside point with zero net force.

== Proof ==

Assume a '''uniform thin spherical shell''': radius $R$, total mass $M$, and surface density $\sigma=M/(4\pi R^2)$.

Put the shell centre at $O$. A point $P$ is at distance $r$ from $O$. Set $z$-axis along $\overrightarrow{OP}$

[[File:Shell-theorem.ggb]]

Take a thin ring on the shell at angle $\theta$ from $OP$.

* Ring radius: $R\sin\theta$
* Ring width: $R\,d\theta$
* Ring area:

$$
dA=(2\pi R\sin\theta)(R\,d\theta)=2\pi R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta
$$

* Ring mass:

$$
dM=\sigma dA
=\frac{M}{4\pi R^2}\,2\pi R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta
=\frac{M}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta
$$

Distance from the ring to $P$:

$$
s=\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rR\cos\theta}
$$

Gravitational potential at $P$:

$$
\Phi(r)=-G\int \frac{dM}{s}
$$

So

$$
\Phi(r)
=
-\frac{GM}{2}
\int_0^\pi
\frac{\sin\theta\,d\theta}
{\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rR\cos\theta}}
$$

Let

$$
u=\cos\theta,\qquad du=-\sin\theta\,d\theta
$$

Then

$$
\Phi(r)
=
-\frac{GM}{2}
\int_{-1}^{1}
\frac{du}
{\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rRu}}
$$

Evaluate the integral:

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}
\frac{du}
{\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rRu}}
=
-\frac{1}{rR}
\left[
\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rRu}
\right]_{-1}^{1}
$$

Now split into two cases:

=== 1. Outside the shell: $r>R$ ===

At $u=1$,

$$
\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rR}=|r-R|=r-R
$$

At $u=-1$,

$$
\sqrt{r^2+R^2+2rR}=r+R
$$

So

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}
\frac{du}{\sqrt{\cdots}}
=
-\frac{1}{rR}\big[(r-R)-(r+R)\big]
=
-\frac{1}{rR}(-2R)
=
\frac{2}{r}
$$

Thus

$$
\Phi(r)
=
-\frac{GM}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{r}
=
-\frac{GM}{r}
$$

This is exactly the potential of a point mass $M$ at the centre.

Therefore the force on a small mass $m$ outside is

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{F}
=
-G\frac{Mm}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf{r}}
}
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Outside a uniform spherical shell, gravity is the same as if all mass were at the centre.}
}
$$

=== 2. Inside the shell: $r<R$ ===

At $u=1$,

$$
\sqrt{r^2+R^2-2rR}=|r-R|=R-r
$$

At $u=-1$,

$$
\sqrt{r^2+R^2+2rR}=r+R
$$

So

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}
\frac{du}{\sqrt{\cdots}}
=
-\frac{1}{rR}\big[(R-r)-(r+R)\big]
=
-\frac{1}{rR}(-2r)
=
\frac{2}{R}
$$

Thus

$$
\Phi(r)
=
-\frac{GM}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{R}
=
-\frac{GM}{R}
$$

Which is constant regardless of value of $r$.

Therefore

$$
\nabla \Phi = 0
$$

hence the gravitational field is zero:

$$
\mathbf{g}=-\nabla\Phi=0
$$

So the force on any mass inside the shell is zero

$$
\boxed{\mathbf{F}_g=0}
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Inside a uniform spherical shell, the net gravitational force is zero.}
}
$$

== Application on spherically symmetric solids ==

Approximate the solid (S) as the sum of many thin spherical shells:

* For any point, the gravitational pull from the solid is identical to that of a point mass at its center
* For a point P outside the solid: $m_{\text{point mass}}=m_{(S)}$
* For a point Q within the solid: $m_{\text{point mass}}=\int_{0}^{P}\rho(r)4\pi r^2dr$ (mass of part of S contained by $\bigcirc _{r=\overrightarrow{OQ}}$)
